'''Fufu''' (or '''fufuo''', '''foofoo''', '''foufou''' {{IPAc-en|'|f|u|,|f|u}} {{Respell|foo|foo}} {{pronunciation|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Izundu Okechukwu-Fufu.wav|listen|}}) is a pounded meal found in [[West African cuisine]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Ukegbu |first=Kavachi Michelle |title=The art of fufu : a guide to the culture and flavors of a West African tradition |date=2021 |others=Grubido |isbn=978-1-62634-596-6 |location=Austin, Texas |oclc=1241244901}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=5 Popular Swallows Eaten By Ghanaians |url=https://www.modernghana.com/lifestyle/10257/5-popular-swallows-eaten-by-ghanaians.html |access-date=2022-05-03 |website=Modern Ghana |language=en}}</ref> originally made from boiled [[cassava]], [[Cooking banana|plantains]], and [[cocoyam]]. Fufu's prevalence in West Africa has been noted in local [[literature]], such as [[Chinua Achebe]]'s ''[[Things Fall Apart]]''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Achebe |first=Chinua |url=http://archive.org/details/thingsfallapart00ache_ldx |title=Things fall apart |date=1994 |publisher=New York : Anchor Books |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-385-47454-2}}</ref>

It is a [[Twi]] word originating from the [[Akan people|Akans]] in [[Ghana]], but the word has been expanded to include several variations of the pounded meal found in other African countries including [[Sierra Leone]],  [[Liberia]], [[Ivory Coast]], [[Burkina Faso]], [[Benin]], [[Togo]], [[Nigeria]], [[Cameroon]], the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Democratic Republic of Congo]], the [[Central African Republic]], the [[Republic of the Congo|Republic of Congo]], [[Angola]] and [[Gabon]]. It also includes variations in the [[Greater Antilles]] and [[Central America]], where African culinary influence is high.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Victoria |first=Akinola |date=2022-04-24 |title=5 Nigerian meals that have similar versions across African countries |url=https://www.pulse.ng/lifestyle/food-travel/5-nigerian-meals-that-have-similar-versions-across-african-countries/zj9jv8k |access-date=2022-05-03 |newspaper=[[Pulse Nigeria]]|language=en}}</ref> 

In Ghana, Ivory Coast, and Liberia, they use the method of separately mixing and pounding equal portions of boiled cassava with green plantain or cocoyam, or by mixing cassava/plantain/cocoyam flour with water and stirring it on a stove. Its thickness is then adjusted to personal preference, and it is eaten with [[broth]]-like soups. Meanwhile, in Nigeria fufu is made solely from fermented cassava, giving it its unique thickness compared to that found elsewhere. It is eaten with a variety of soups (such as [[Egusi soup]] and [[Ogbono soup]]), vegetables, beef, and fish.<ref name="Nweke">{{cite web|last1=Nweke|first1=Felix I.|title=THE CASSAVA TRANSFORMATION IN AFRICA|url=https://www.fao.org/docrep/009/a0154e/A0154E02.HTM |publisher=United Nations|access-date=10 June 2014}}</ref> 

In recent years other flours, such as [[semolina|wheat semolina]], [[maize|maize flour]], or mashed plantains may take the place of cassava flour. This is common for those in the [[diaspora]] or families that live in urban cities. Families in rural areas with access to farmland still maintain the original recipe of using cassava. Fufu is traditionally eaten with the fingers, and a small ball of it can be dipped into an accompanying soup or sauce.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is Fufu, the West African Delicacy? |url=https://www.finedininglovers.com/article/fufu-what-is-it-how-to-eat-it |access-date=2022-09-17 |website=www.finedininglovers.com |language=en}}</ref>
